# Marcus

Marcus has been cutting hair for thirty-four years. He knows the rhythms of his work the way a musician knows their instrument—the weight of scissors in his palm, the angle of the blade, the way different textures of hair respond to his touch. His small shop sits on a corner in the neighborhood where he's lived most of his adult life, and his clients are people he's known for decades. Some have been coming to him since they were boys themselves.

Three years ago, on a Tuesday evening in October, Marcus was closing up. He'd just finished sweeping, the smell of hair tonic and soap still hanging in the air, when two men pushed through the door. He remembers their faces clearly—something he wishes he didn't. One held a knife. The other went straight for the register while the man with the blade kept the knife pointed at Marcus's chest, telling him not to move, not to look at them, not to do anything stupid. Marcus complied. He'd heard stories, knew better than to resist. It was over in minutes. They took the day's cash—about three hundred dollars—and left him standing alone in his shop, shaking.

The police came. They took a report. They never found the men.

Now, three years later, Marcus still closes his shop at four o'clock instead of six. He tells his wife, Amara, it's because he's getting older, wants more time at home. The truth is different. As the sun begins to set, his chest tightens. He finds himself checking the locks repeatedly, positioning himself so he can see the door. His hands shake. He's stopped working on Tuesdays altogether, though he doesn't acknowledge why.

When clients come in, Marcus struggles to concentrate. His mind splits between the present—the familiar weight of scissors, the small talk about grandchildren and work—and the past. He finds himself studying new customers' hands, looking for weapons. Last month, a young man came in wearing a dark jacket, and Marcus's vision narrowed. His breathing became shallow. He made an excuse and stepped into the back room for ten minutes, gripping the edge of the sink until the panic subsided.

At night, Marcus lies awake beside Amara, his body rigid with tension. When he does sleep, he dreams of the knife, of his own helplessness. He wakes gasping, sometimes shouting. Amara has learned not to touch him when he first wakes; his startle response is severe. She lies quietly, waiting for him to recognize where he is.

He's become irritable with Amara over small things—a noise she makes while eating, a question about his day. Then guilt washes over him. She doesn't deserve this. He knows that. He apologizes, but the anger returns unpredictably, a storm he can't control.

Marcus has lost weight. He used to enjoy the meals Amara prepared, but now food tastes like nothing. He's withdrawn from his friends, declined invitations to the monthly poker game he'd played in for twenty years. The thought of being in a crowded room, unable to see all the exits, makes his stomach clench.

He hasn't told anyone about the nightmares, the hypervigilance, the way he sometimes feels like he's back in that shop, frozen and powerless. He tells himself he should be over it by now. He survived. No one was hurt. But the fear remains, coiled inside him, waiting.
